lead: An assembler converts assembly source into machine code. A simulator runs that machine code on a PC without the chip. An IDE joins an editor, assembler, downloader and debugger in one window. Together they form the development tool chain for 8085, 8086 and 8051 programs. You write mnemonics, the assembler gives bytes and a hex file, and the simulator or board runs the bytes. This chapter shows how labels become addresses, which files are produced, and how a debugger helps find mistakes before hardware is used.
prereq: You need: instruction encoding from 3.1 and program structure from 3.7.

blocks.text: An assembler is a program that translates assembly source into machine code. It turns each mnemonic into an opcode and each label into an address. A directive is a command to the assembler, not an instruction to the CPU. ORG n sets the location counter to n. The location counter (LC) is the address the assembler will give to the next byte it emits. DB places byte constants in memory. DW places 16-bit words, low byte first on the 8085 and 8086. EQU gives a name a fixed value. END marks the end of the source, and lines after it are ignored.

items: A label is entered in the symbol table with the current LC; it emits no bytes.
An instruction is encoded from its opcode table and operand; the LC advances by the instruction length.
A directive changes the LC, data or symbols; only DB and DW emit bytes.

blocks.text: Most assemblers use two passes. Pass 1 reads every line and records labels in the symbol table. Pass 2 encodes instructions, now that every label value is known. Only a few universities teach assembler construction in detail; for exams know the two passes, the LC and the symbol table. Some syllabi call the assembler, simulator and IDE together the development tool chain.

sections.h3: Symbol table, object files and hex files

blocks.text: The symbol table maps each label or EQU name to a number. START = 2000H means the label START is address 2000H. The LC is the running address during assembly. A forward reference is a label used before its line is read; pass 1 saves the name, and pass 2 fills in the value.

An object file holds machine code plus symbol and relocation information. A hex file is a plain-text record of addresses and bytes, often in Intel HEX format. The hex file itself has no labels, so on its own a simulator shows addresses only; loading the assembler's symbol file lets it show label names. A linker joins several object files into one program and resolves labels that are external. For a single small program the assembler can output a hex file directly.

A cross-assembler runs on a PC but produces code for another processor, such as an 8085 or 8051. That is normal because the target board cannot run an editor or assembler. The produced hex file is copied to the board by a device programmer (a hardware unit that writes the hex file into the chip).

A simulator is software that executes the machine code without the chip. It models registers, flags, memory and I/O. You can set a breakpoint, single-step one instruction, and watch the program counter and flags. A debugger is the part that gives these controls; a simulator usually includes one.

An IDE (integrated development environment) puts editor, assembler, downloader and debugger in one window. You type source, press Build, then Run or Debug. For a board, the downloader sends the hex file to the chip through a serial or USB programmer. For a simulator, the same hex file runs on the PC.
Use a simulator first for loops and delays. Use the board when ports, timers or interrupts matter, because those depend on real hardware.

spec.title: Assembly tool chain
spec.aria: Assembly source goes through the assembler to an object or hex file, which is then run on a simulator or board.

examples.question: Assemble this 8085 source. Give the location counter after each line, the symbol table, and the bytes in memory: ORG 2000H / START: MVI A,05H / LOOP: DCR A / JNZ LOOP / END
steps: ORG 2000H sets LC = 2000H and emits no bytes.
START is entered as 2000H. MVI A,05H is 2 bytes: 3E at 2000H and 05 at 2001H. LC becomes 2002H.
LOOP is entered as 2002H. DCR A is 1 byte: 3D at 2002H. LC becomes 2003H.
JNZ LOOP is 3 bytes: C2, low target 02, high target 20 at 2003H, 2004H and 2005H. The target is LOOP = 2002H. LC becomes 2006H.
END is a directive and emits no bytes.
examples.answer: The assembled bytes are 3E 05 3D C2 02 20 at addresses 2000H to 2005H; symbols are START = 2000H and LOOP = 2002H.
examples.check:
print(int('2000', 16))
print(int('2002', 16))
print(int('3E', 16))
print(int('05', 16))
print(int('3D', 16))
print(int('C2', 16))
print(int('02', 16))
print(int('20', 16))

traps: ORG sets the location counter; it does not load bytes into memory. A loader or simulator places the hex file at the address.
Labels such as START are addresses, not instructions. A label line emits no opcode.
EQU and END are assembler directives; they are not CPU instructions and have no opcodes.
In JNZ LOOP the target is the address of LOOP (2002H in the example), not the address of JNZ (2003H) and not the next instruction.
DW stores a 16-bit word low byte first on the 8085 and 8086. Writing DW 1234H puts 34H before 12H.

quiz.q: What does the ORG directive do?
quiz.a: ORG n sets the location counter to n, so the next emitted byte gets address n. It does not itself write memory.
A table built by the assembler that maps each label or EQU name to its address or value.

quiz.q: Why does an assembler usually make two passes?
quiz.a: Pass 1 records labels and their addresses in the symbol table. Pass 2 encodes instructions using those label values, including forward references.

quiz.q: Assemble: ORG 2500H / L: MVI B,0FH / NOP / JMP L. Give the bytes and the value of L.
A JNZ instruction is at 2003H and jumps to LOOP = 2010H. Give its three bytes.
quiz.a: JNZ opcode is C2. The low byte is 10 and the high byte is 20. Bytes: C2 10 20.

quiz.q: State two differences between a simulator and a target board.
quiz.a: A simulator runs code in software and shows registers and memory without hardware. A board runs the real chip, so ports, timers and voltage levels are real.

quiz.q: A program is assembled with ORG 2000H and contains JMP 2500H, written as a fixed absolute address, not a label. You change the ORG to 3000H and reassemble. Why may the program now fail?
quiz.a: The bytes of the JMP operand are still 00 25, so the jump goes to 2500H. That address is now empty because the code moved to 3000H. Absolute addresses do not move with the program; only labels recomputed by the assembler move.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern toolchains use GNU as and ld, Keil, MPLAB X or Arduino's avr-gcc, often with JTAG or SWD debug probes. Simulators are used in continuous integration to run firmware tests without boards. Search for GNU assembler directives, Intel HEX format and JTAG debug to go deeper.
